content: Why do some groups of notes sound smooth while others sound like a mistake? I have always thought dissonance simply means someone played the wrong notes, but certain songs seem to use those sounds on purpose.

Dissonance is not the same as error. It describes a kind of instability or friction listeners often hear between notes. Composers use that friction deliberately, much as a story uses suspense. Consonant combinations tend to feel settled; dissonant ones often create an expectation of movement, though context can strengthen or weaken that effect.
What makes the friction happen in the first place? Are the sound waves actually bumping into each other, or is smoothness just a name people give to note groups they already know?

Both acoustics and familiarity matter. A musical tone contains a main vibration plus higher partials. When partials from two notes nearly coincide, their loudness can pulse or sound rough; when many align neatly, the blend is often smoother. Learned musical patterns then shape whether that blend feels stable, expected, tense, or unfamiliar.
Why would a simple pair like a fifth sound especially settled, then? I hear people say the waves fit together, but I cannot picture what is fitting or how often it repeats.

In an ideally tuned fifth, the upper note vibrates about three times while the lower vibrates twice. Their combined wave pattern therefore repeats quickly, and several strong partials coincide. That regularity helps the ear combine them into a stable whole. It is a useful explanation, although musical context still affects how settled the interval feels.
So does a messier number relationship automatically make a chord wrong? If a composer leaves a rough chord hanging at the end, I assume the music has failed to finish properly.

A more complex relationship may increase roughness, but it does not make the chord wrong. Ending on tension can be an intentional choice: it may suggest uncertainty, interruption, or openness. Whether the ending feels incomplete depends on the style, the preceding harmony, the listener's expectations, and how the notes are voiced.
Why does a minor chord sound sad if minor keys are basically sad versions of major keys? I assume the chord becomes dissonant when its middle note is lowered, and that roughness creates the sadness.

A minor triad is usually treated as consonant, not dissonant. Lowering the third changes the interval pattern and the chord's color, but it does not simply add acoustic roughness. The common link between minor and sadness comes strongly from musical convention, tempo, melody, rhythm, and performance; a minor chord can also sound calm, serious, tender, or forceful.
What exactly changes when that middle note moves down? The outside notes can stay the same, so I would expect the chord to keep the same basic feeling with one slightly darker note inside.

The root and fifth can remain fixed, but the third tells the ear whether the triad is major or minor. Lowering it changes two relationships at once: the root-to-third interval shrinks, while the third-to-fifth interval grows. That rearrangement changes the chord's identity even though its outer frame remains a perfect fifth.
Does that mean major and minor chords are equally smooth in a physical sense? One still seems brighter to me, so I keep wanting brightness to mean the waves line up better.

They can both sound smooth, although their partials do not align in exactly the same way, especially on real instruments and in equal temperament. Brightness is not a direct meter of consonance. Register, timbre, loudness, voicing, and learned associations all contribute to the brighter-major and darker-minor contrast.
Why can a fast song in a minor key sound playful, then? If the key supplies the sadness, I would think changing the beat could decorate that feeling but not reverse it.

A key supplies a set of tonal relationships, not a fixed emotion. Fast tempo, springy rhythm, rising melodic shapes, light articulation, and bright instruments can outweigh the associations of the minor third. The result may sound playful or energetic while still being recognizably in a minor key.
Then what should I listen for if I want to separate consonance from mood? I tend to call any comfortable sound happy and any uneasy sound sad, which seems too simple now.

Listen first for stability rather than emotion. Does the chord seem able to rest, or does it pull toward another chord? Then notice its sensory roughness: are there audible pulses or clashes? Finally name the mood separately. A chord can be stable yet somber, or tense yet exciting, so those judgments need not match.
What is the wobbling sound I hear when two nearby piano notes are played together? I am certain that wobble means one of the notes is wrong, because a correct chord should hold a steady sound.

That wobble is called beating. When two frequencies are close but not identical, their waves alternately reinforce and partly cancel one another, producing regular changes in loudness. It can reveal mistuning, but it can also occur between intentionally chosen notes or between their overtones, so it is not proof of a mistake.
Why do the beats speed up when the notes move farther apart at first? I would have guessed that separating them should stop the interference and make the sound smoother right away.

The beat rate equals the difference between the two frequencies. If one tone is 440 vibrations per second and the other is 442, you hear about two beats each second. Increasing the gap increases that rate until the pulses become too fast to hear separately and merge into a rough texture.
Is that rough texture what dissonance is, or can a chord feel unsettled without any obvious buzzing? I use those two reactions as if they were the same thing.

Roughness is one source of dissonance, but the terms are not identical. A chord can have little audible beating yet feel unstable because of its role in a key. Conversely, two tones can sound rough in a particular register or timbre without creating a strong expectation that the harmony must move somewhere.
Could I make a dissonant pair seem smoother just by playing it more quietly? If the wobble becomes harder to notice, I assume the notes effectively turn consonant.

Lowering the volume can reduce the harshness you perceive, especially when the sound is dense or distorted, but it does not change the interval or its harmonic function. You may hear less sensory roughness while still hearing the pair as unstable. Consonance has acoustic, musical, and perceptual parts rather than one switch.
Why can the same chord sound peaceful in one song and tense in another? Dissonance should mean wrong notes, so I would expect the chord itself to carry that label wherever it appears.

A chord's effect depends partly on what surrounds it. The key establishes a tonal center, and the preceding chords create expectations about what should follow. A chord that serves as a resting point in one setting may act as a step toward another chord elsewhere. Its notes stay the same, but its function changes.
What does a chord actually do to point toward another one? I understand a melody moving upward, but a stack of notes seems stationary once it has been played.

Individual notes inside the chord can sit close to notes in a likely destination chord. The ear follows those small motions, especially half-step movements. Scale patterns also make certain chord roots feel temporary and others central. The chord does not physically move; learned expectations make particular continuations sound more directed and satisfying.
Is that why the chord built on the fifth note seems to want the first chord? I assume every note in it must move downward together to release the tension.

The dominant chord often leads to the tonic, but its notes do not all move downward. In a common voicing, the leading tone rises by a half step to the tonic, while another active note may fall by a step. The bass often moves from scale degree five to one, creating a strong root motion.
Why does adding the extra seventh make that pull stronger? Is the added note simply more wrong than the others, or does it create a particular short move the ear expects?

The added seventh creates a tritone with the chord's third, increasing instability, and it also supplies another clear tendency tone. In common tonal writing, that seventh usually steps downward while the leading tone steps upward. Those opposite half-step resolutions make the destination chord especially easy to anticipate.
Could a song refuse both of those little moves and keep going somewhere else? I would think the unresolved notes remain mistakes until they eventually reach their usual places.

It can refuse, delay, or redirect them. A deceptive cadence sends the dominant somewhere unexpected; jazz may reinterpret a tense note as part of the next chord; other styles may value suspended motion. The expectation still helps create the effect, but breaking an expectation intentionally is not the same as making an error.
Then is consonance mainly the moment when expectations stop, rather than a special sound in the notes themselves? I am trying to tell whether context or wave shape matters more.

Neither explanation works alone. Sensory consonance concerns features such as beating and overtone alignment; tonal consonance concerns stability inside a musical system. They often support each other, but not always. A useful listening test is to compare the same interval by itself, inside several chords, and at the end of different progressions.
Why does the same pair of notes sound clean on one instrument and harsh on another? If the pitches are correct, I believe any harshness must mean the player accidentally added wrong notes.

Each instrument produces more than the named pitches. Its tone includes a particular mixture of overtones, noise, and changes over time. Those extra components can align, beat, or crowd one another differently. A flute playing an interval may sound purer than a distorted guitar playing the same interval without either performer choosing a wrong pitch.
What are those extra sounds if I still hear one note from each instrument? Are they tiny hidden notes above the main one, or just different shapes of the same vibration?

Both descriptions point toward the same phenomenon. A complex repeating vibration can be analyzed as a fundamental frequency plus partials above it. The ear usually groups that collection into one pitch with a distinctive tone color. Because instruments emphasize different partials, their versions of one named note need not interact identically with another note.
Why would distortion make an ordinary chord seem more crowded? I thought an amplifier only made the existing sound louder, so it should preserve which combinations are consonant.

Clean amplification mainly raises level, but distortion reshapes the waveform and creates new partials. With several notes, it can also generate combination tones not present in either note alone. These added frequencies may clash closely, especially in full chords, which is why distorted guitar parts often favor open fifths over dense triads.
Is an open fifth missing its middle note because that note would be wrong under distortion? It sounds complete enough, so perhaps the middle part of a chord is optional decoration.

The third is not wrong; omitting it reduces spectral crowding and leaves the harmony ambiguous between major and minor. Under strong distortion, a root and fifth already generate a rich set of overtones. The third can be added when its color is wanted, but the cleaner two-note shape is often easier to hear.
Could a composer choose instrument sounds first and then decide which chords count as smooth? I had assumed the consonance rules stayed fixed before the instruments entered the picture.

Yes. Arrangement and harmony influence each other. A chord that is clear in soft, separated timbres may become rough in bright, sustained ones. Composers can change spacing, register, doubling, or instrumentation while keeping the chord name. The underlying intervals matter, but their audible treatment helps determine the final degree of consonance.

What makes people agree that some chords are consonant if musical customs differ? I think dissonance must still mean objectively wrong notes, because otherwise every combination would sound equally acceptable somewhere.

Listeners share hearing mechanisms, so combinations with strong beating or dense frequency interactions often have broadly similar effects. But musical systems teach people how to classify, use, and expect those sounds. That produces overlap without complete agreement. Dissonance can be perceptually rough, culturally unstable, or both, and none of those meanings automatically means wrong.
Why would hearing a certain sound many times make it less dissonant? The waves have not changed, so I would expect the same physical clash to remain just as strong.

Repeated exposure does not remove acoustic beating, but it can change interpretation and expectation. A once-surprising chord may become a familiar color or a normal resting sound within a style. Listeners also learn to group complicated sonorities as units, so perceived tension can decrease even while their physical frequency relationships stay identical.
Does that mean a culture could train people to hear a buzzing interval as completely smooth? I am unsure where the ear's physical limit ends and learned taste begins.

Learning can make rough sounds valued, familiar, or stable, but it does not necessarily erase the sensation of roughness. Think of spicy food: enjoyment and sensory intensity can change somewhat independently. Musical training and exposure adjust categories and expectations, while the ear's mechanics continue responding to nearby frequency components.
What about music that uses notes between piano keys? I assume those tones are out of tune versions of the real notes, so any chords made from them should be especially wrong.

Piano pitches belong to one tuning system, not the only set of real notes. Other traditions divide pitch space differently or vary notes expressively. Their intervals can form stable relationships within their own frameworks. Calling them out of tune only makes sense relative to a specified tuning, instrument, or musical expectation.
How can I compare two systems without quietly treating the piano as the standard? Should I listen for beating, for where phrases rest, or for which note returns most often?

Use several clues separately. Beating tells you about close acoustic interactions; repeated destinations suggest tonal centers; phrase endings reveal stability; and performers' tuning choices show which relationships they favor. Most importantly, learn the system's own categories and functions instead of translating every sound immediately into the nearest piano key.
If two traditions classify the same interval differently, is one hearing it incorrectly? I keep thinking there must be a final scientific label that settles whether the sound itself is consonant.

Science can measure frequency ratios, beating, auditory masking, and listener responses, but the word consonant combines several judgments. Two traditions can assign different functions to the same measured sound without either mishearing it. Clear discussion specifies whether it means low roughness, tonal stability, pleasantness, or accepted usage in a style.
So why do basic explanations list fixed consonant and dissonant intervals? That kind of chart makes the boundary look permanent, with no room for the music around each pair.

Those charts summarize conventions for a particular style, usually common-practice Western harmony, and they help listeners predict typical treatment. They are maps, not universal laws. A fuller account adds tuning, timbre, register, historical period, and harmonic context, turning a rigid two-column list into a graded and conditional description.
Why does an octave sound almost like the same note while a half-step sounds like a clash? I assume the half-step contains one correct note and one nearby wrong version of it.

An octave has a simple two-to-one frequency relationship, so many partials of the upper tone coincide with partials of the lower. The ear often groups them as versions of one pitch class. A half-step places many strong components close enough to interfere and also has a less simple relationship, but both notes can be intentional and correct.
What does the two-to-one part mean in ordinary sound? If the higher note vibrates twice, does every second bump land exactly on one bump from the lower note?

That is a useful picture. During one cycle of the lower vibration, the upper completes two cycles, so their combined pattern lines up and repeats after each lower cycle. Real instrument waves are more complicated than simple bumps, but their harmonic partials preserve much of that regular alignment.
Why is a fifth also smooth if its notes are not versions of the same note name? Does its pattern repeat almost as neatly, just after a slightly longer wait?

Yes. A pure fifth has a three-to-two ratio, so its joint pattern repeats after two cycles of the lower tone and three of the upper. That is still a short repeat, and several partials overlap. The fifth retains two distinct pitch identities, yet their relationship is highly regular.
Then why not rank every interval only by how long its combined pattern takes to repeat? That seems like it should give one exact ladder from smooth to wrong.

Ratio simplicity explains part of the pattern, especially for steady harmonic tones, but it misses timbre, register, tuning, loudness, and musical function. Equal-tempered intervals are also slightly adjusted from pure ratios. Consonance is therefore graded and context-sensitive, not an exact ladder from mathematically simple to musically wrong.
What changes when a third note is added to a smooth pair? I think minor chords are just sad major chords, so the middle note seems to control mood rather than how the chord itself blends.

Adding the third creates two new relationships and distinguishes common major and minor triads. Lowering it does more than attach sadness: it changes the root-to-third and third-to-fifth intervals, altering the chord quality. Both triads can be consonant, while their emotional effects depend strongly on the surrounding music.
Why do the root, third, and fifth usually blend, then? There are three pairs inside that stack, and I would expect at least one pair to rub against another.

In major and minor triads, the outer notes form a perfect fifth, while the middle note forms thirds with its neighbors. Those intervals are familiar and moderately smooth in common tuning. Their partials do not all coincide, but the total pattern avoids the strongest close clashes in a comfortable register.
What makes a diminished chord sound less settled if it is still built by stacking thirds? I assumed using the same building method would give it the same amount of smoothness.

Its outer notes form a diminished fifth, or tritone, instead of a perfect fifth. That changes the acoustic blend and gives the chord stronger directional tendencies in tonal music. The two thirds are also both minor, so the stack is symmetrical and does not establish a root as firmly as a major or minor triad.
Is the middle note still the problem because it helps make both small thirds? If I moved only that note, could I turn the chord into something settled without changing its base?

You could move the middle note and create another chord, but it is not uniquely at fault. Keeping the bottom and top fixes the tritone, so those outer notes would still carry much of the instability. To form a standard major or minor triad, you would usually change one of the outer notes.
Why can adding a fourth note sometimes make a tense chord sound richer instead of simply worse? More note pairs should create more chances for clashes, so I expect a steady decline.

More notes do create more interval relationships, but their effect is not simple addition. A seventh or ninth can clarify a chord's function, spread tension across a recognizable color, or connect smoothly to surrounding voices. Good spacing also prevents crowding. Complexity can make tension more intelligible rather than merely harsher.
Why do chords sound muddy when played low but clearer when moved upward? I thought dissonance meant hitting wrong notes, so changing only the height should not fix the chord.

Low notes have partials packed into frequency regions where the ear has more difficulty separating nearby components. Close chord tones can therefore create strong roughness and obscure the bass line. Moving the same chord upward spreads relevant frequencies perceptually, so its identity becomes clearer even though the note names and chord label remain unchanged.
What does packed together mean if the notes keep the same distance on the keyboard? A third is the same number of keys everywhere, so I assumed the spacing was physically identical.

Keyboard distance measures pitch steps, not a fixed difference in vibrations per second. Each octave doubles frequency. A low third may differ by only a few dozen hertz, while the same interval high up differs by hundreds. The ear's frequency resolution also varies across its range, making low close intervals more prone to roughness.
Is that why players leave a wide gap above the lowest note? It looks like the chord is missing pieces near the bottom, but perhaps those notes are moved elsewhere.

Exactly. A common voicing places the bass note alone or with a fifth, then puts thirds and other colorful tones higher. The chord still contains the information needed for its identity, but its components occupy clearer ranges. This spacing is called open voicing when compared with notes packed closely together.
Would spreading every chord as widely as possible always make it more consonant? I imagine enough distance should prevent all the sound waves from rubbing against one another.

Wider spacing often reduces low-register roughness, but unlimited spread can weaken unity, create awkward melodic leaps, or expose bright upper partials. Notes separated by octaves still interact harmonically. The best spacing depends on instrument, register, chord function, and the desired texture rather than a rule that wider is always smoother.
What if I keep the low chord but play each note one after another? Since they no longer happen together, does the dissonance disappear or merely turn into a different kind of tension?

Separating the notes reduces simultaneous beating, especially if earlier tones fade quickly. Yet the listener may remember them as one harmony, so tonal tension can remain. An arpeggio can make a dense chord more transparent without changing its harmonic identity, showing again that sensory roughness and functional instability are related but distinct.
Why does holding the pedal bring the muddiness back even when I play the notes separately? I thought separate attacks would stop them from becoming a real chord.

The sustain pedal lets earlier strings keep vibrating while later notes arrive, so their sounds overlap and recreate much of the simultaneous spectrum. Resonance can add still more sympathetic vibrations. Separate attacks change the beginning of each tone, but sustained overlap allows the ear to combine them into a chord-like mass.
What happens to consonance when a chord is played very loudly? I believe a correct chord should stay smooth at any volume, while harshness at high volume means someone included a wrong note.

Loudness can change perceived roughness even when every pitch stays fixed. At higher levels, each frequency component affects a broader region of hearing, so neighboring components interfere more. Instruments and speakers may also produce distortion when pushed. The harmony remains the same on paper, but its sensory impact can become harsher.
Why does playing the notes gently and one after another make the same chord feel softer? Is that only because less sound reaches the ear, or does timing change the chord itself?

Both level and timing matter. Gentle attacks contain less abrupt high-frequency energy, while staggered entries prevent every transient from piling up at once. The chord's pitch collection remains, but its texture changes. Your ear can follow each line more easily, often making a harmonically tense sonority feel less aggressive.
Is a sharp attack another form of dissonance, then? A struck note can sound biting before it settles, even when no second pitch is being played beside it.

A sharp attack can be noisy or bright without being harmonically dissonant. At the start of a note, many irregular or high-frequency components briefly appear before the steady tone develops. That sensory harshness resembles chordal roughness, but it comes from timbre over time rather than an unstable relationship between named pitches.
Could a performer make a normally dissonant chord seem calm without changing its notes? I assume the chord would still be technically wrong, but perhaps the delivery could hide that fact.

A performer can make it calmer through soft dynamics, gradual attacks, careful balance, wider spacing, and gentle resolution. The chord remains whatever harmonic structure it was, but it was never technically wrong merely for being dissonant. Performance shapes whether its tension feels piercing, suspended, warm, mysterious, or almost weightless.
Why are piano chords accepted as in tune when their intervals are not perfectly pure? I assumed any note adjusted away from the exact ratio becomes a wrong note and therefore adds dissonance.

Modern pianos usually use equal temperament, which divides the octave into twelve equal pitch steps. Except for the octave, its intervals differ slightly from simple whole-number ratios. Those small compromises let musicians play in every key without retuning, and listeners generally accept the mild beating as part of the instrument's normal sound.
What is being shared equally in equal temperament? I picture the tuner spreading one fixed amount of error among all twelve notes, but I do not know what is measured.

The octave's frequency ratio of two to one is divided into twelve equal multiplicative steps. Each neighboring key has the same ratio, the twelfth root of two, rather than the same number of hertz. The compromise is not equal audible error in every interval; it is equal semitone spacing on a logarithmic scale.
Why does a tuned fifth still sound smooth if it misses the simple three-to-two match? Should there not be a steady wobble warning that the two notes do not belong together?

An equal-tempered fifth is only about two cents narrower than a pure fifth, so the mismatch is small. Some upper partials beat slowly, but the interval keeps most of its strong alignment and familiar stability. On a piano, the natural decay and slightly inharmonic strings also affect whether that beating stands out.
Could a singer remove the wobble by bending one note into a pure ratio? I assume that would make the chord universally more consonant, no matter what comes next.

Singers often adjust sustained notes toward smoother ratios, especially in unaccompanied ensembles. That can reduce beating in the current chord. But a note may also need to connect melodically, match a fixed-pitch instrument, or prepare another harmony, so the acoustically pure choice at one moment is not always best for the larger phrase.
Then what does out of tune mean if the target can move with the chord? I have been using it as another name for dissonant, but those seem to separate here.

Out of tune means a performed pitch misses the intended target, and that target depends on the tuning practice and musical situation. Dissonant describes a perceived or functional relationship among sounds. A perfectly tuned interval can be deliberately dissonant, while a slightly mistuned consonance can still be recognized as the intended consonant interval.
Why can a melody use a note that is not in the chord without sounding mistaken? I have always believed dissonance means wrong notes, so the tune should clash whenever it steps outside the chord.

Melodies often use non-chord tones to connect, decorate, or delay the chord tones. Their timing and motion tell the ear how to understand them. A brief passing note between two stable notes can be dissonant against the accompaniment yet sound completely intentional because its approach and departure form a clear pattern.
What makes one outside note sound like a passing note rather than a mistake? Is it mainly shortness, or does it have to move in a certain direction afterward?

Short duration helps, but placement and motion are crucial. A passing tone usually fills the step between two chord tones, often on a weaker beat. A neighboring tone steps away and returns. When the line follows one of these recognizable shapes, the ear hears purposeful movement rather than an isolated pitch choice.
Why does the same note feel more awkward when it lands on the strong beat? The pitch against the chord is identical, so I would expect the clash to have the same weight.

A strong beat gives the note emphasis and makes listeners treat it as structurally important. The same interval held there demands more explanation than a quick weak-beat connection. Composers exploit this with suspensions, placing a dissonance prominently and then resolving it by step, so greater awkwardness can become greater expressiveness.
What is suspended in a suspension? I picture the melody pausing in the air while the chord changes underneath, but I am not sure which sound creates the tension.

That picture is close. A note from the previous chord is held, or suspended, while the other voices move to a new chord. The held note now forms a dissonant interval against the new harmony. It then usually steps to a chord tone, making the preparation, clash, and resolution easy to hear.
If the held note never resolves, does it become a wrong note after enough time? I assume intentional tension has a deadline before it counts as an error.

There is no universal deadline. In one style, a suspension may resolve quickly; in another, the unresolved color may become the stable sonority itself. Duration changes expectation, but intention is communicated through the whole pattern: repetition, instrumentation, later harmony, and stylistic language can all make a lasting tension sound deliberate.
How would I tell a deliberate unresolved note from an accidental one just by listening? Both could stay in place, and I cannot inspect what the composer meant.

You cannot always know intention from sound alone. Look for evidence of pattern: does the note recur, connect smoothly to a line, match the style, or receive a meaningful later response? An accidental pitch may disrupt those patterns, but even accidents can sound convincing. Musical correctness is partly inferred, not directly contained in one frequency.
What makes the interval called a tritone sound so uneasy? I assume its old nickname means the two notes are especially wrong and should never appear inside a proper chord.

A tritone spans six semitones, exactly half an equal-tempered octave. Its frequency relationship is less simple than an octave or fifth, and its partials can interact roughly. More importantly, tonal music gives its two notes strong tendencies to move inward or outward by half steps. It is useful precisely because it creates direction.
Why does being half an octave not make it balanced and smooth? Half of something even sounds simpler than the three-against-two relationship used for a fifth.

Half the keyboard distance is not half the octave's frequency ratio. Pitch spacing is logarithmic: the octave doubles frequency, and the equal-tempered tritone multiplies it by the square root of two. That ratio is not a small fraction, so the apparent geometric symmetry does not create the overtone alignment heard in a fifth.
Is the tritone inside the usual dominant seventh chord the reason that chord wants to move? I thought the bottom note alone pointed back to the home note.

The bass motion from dominant to tonic matters, but the tritone adds a particularly clear internal pull. Its two notes typically resolve by half step in opposite directions, landing on stable chord tones. This compact voice leading lets the ear recognize the destination even if the chord root is omitted.
Could the same two notes resolve the opposite way and still sound correct? If there is only one proper destination, then other movements would seem like wrong-note dissonance again.

They can resolve in more than one direction. Because a tritone divides the octave symmetrically, the same pitch pair can belong to different dominant seventh chords when spelled or interpreted differently. Composers use that ambiguity for substitution and modulation. The expected destination comes from context, not from the isolated interval alone.

Why does rearranging a chord sometimes change how settled it sounds when the note names stay the same? I believe consonance belongs to the chord label and dissonance means wrong notes, so every ordering should be equally smooth.

A chord label summarizes pitch content, but voicing determines which note is lowest, how far notes are spaced, and which tones are doubled. Those choices change bass stability, overtone interaction, and the motion into the next chord. Two voicings can share a name while differing greatly in weight, clarity, and tension.
What makes putting the third in the bass feel less final than putting the root there? The upper notes are unchanged, so the whole chord should still identify its root clearly.

The chord remains identifiable, but the lowest note strongly shapes how the ear hears its foundation. Root position reinforces the chord's root through bass placement and overtone support. First inversion places the third underneath, producing a lighter, less anchored sonority that often works as a connection between stronger bass positions.
Why does the second inversion sound especially unstable in many simple progressions? I assumed putting the fifth on the bottom would strengthen it because fifths are normally very consonant.

The bass-to-upper-root interval is then a fourth, which common-practice harmony often treats as unstable above the bass. The voicing can also sound like a decorated dominant bass rather than an independent tonic chord. In other styles or rhythmic positions, the same inversion may be perfectly stable, so the rule is contextual.
Does doubling one note make that note twice as important? If I double a tense note, I expect the chord to become twice as dissonant in a fairly direct way.

Doubling increases a pitch's prominence, but musical effects do not scale so neatly. Two performers on the same note may enrich timbre more than loudness, and octave doubling adds aligned partials. Doubling an active tone can emphasize its pull or cause awkward voice leading, yet it does not literally double a consonance score.
Could two different arrangements of the same chord lead to different next chords? I thought the name alone decided where the harmony was allowed to go.

Yes. Each voice tends to continue by a small, singable motion, so a voicing can make one destination especially smooth. Another arrangement may place different notes near different targets or emphasize another bass path. Chord symbols leave those details open; voice leading turns the abstract labels into a particular musical journey.
Why did chords once treated as harsh become ordinary in later music? If dissonance really means playing wrong notes, I assume people simply became less strict about errors over time.

Musical languages change what listeners expect and what composers treat as stable. Sounds can move from rare tension to familiar color through repeated use and new conventions. That does not mean standards disappeared; the standards shifted. A deliberate dissonance follows stylistic patterns, while an error fails to produce the intended pitch or relationship.
What changed first: the chords composers wrote, or the way audiences heard them? I imagine a strange chord must remain wrong until enough people decide to accept it.

The two processes influence each other. Composers introduce or emphasize sonorities, performers make them intelligible, and listeners gradually build expectations from repeated exposure. Earlier music also contains many supposed innovations in different roles. Historical change is usually a long negotiation among practice, hearing, theory, and available instruments.
Why were some fourths called dissonant when a fourth by itself sounds fairly plain to me? Should not the two notes carry the same label whether other voices are present?

In common-practice counterpoint, a perfect fourth above the bass was often treated as dissonant because of its structural role, especially when it suspended a more stable third. Between upper voices, the same interval could be accepted as consonant. The classification described contrapuntal function, not merely isolated pleasantness.
What is the difference between saying an interval is pleasant and saying it is stable? I have been treating both words as softer ways to say that the notes are correct.

Pleasantness is an aesthetic response; stability is an expectation about whether motion is needed. A rough sonority may be enjoyable, and a smooth chord may still feel temporary within a key. Correctness is different again: it concerns whether the sound fits an intention, convention, or performance target. These judgments often overlap but are not interchangeable.
Does a final chord have to be consonant to make the piece feel complete? I assume an ending works only when every tense note reaches a fully correct resting place.

Many tonal pieces end with a stable consonant tonic because that strongly confirms closure. But composers can end on added tones, unresolved chords, noise, or silence to create ambiguity or openness. Completion can also come from rhythm, repetition, fading, or formal return. Harmonic rest is one ending signal, not a requirement.
Were minor keys always heard as sad versions of major keys? I assume lowering the third merely added sadness, so that meaning should stay fixed across historical periods and styles.

No. Major and minor organize intervals differently rather than encoding fixed emotions, and their associations have varied with musical language. Lowering the third is not a built-in sadness control. Mode, cadence, tempo, text, rhythm, and instrumentation can make minor music sound austere, lively, peaceful, threatening, or tender.
What should a consonance chart include if a simple good-versus-bad list is misleading? I still want some way to compare sounds without needing the full history of every piece.

A better chart would separate several dimensions: sensory roughness, ratio simplicity, tonal stability, stylistic treatment, and typical resolution. It could also specify register, tuning, and timbre. You would gain useful default predictions while seeing where they may change, instead of forcing every sound into one permanent category.
So what does the word dissonance usefully tell me on its own? If it covers roughness, instability, and historical rules, I worry it becomes too vague to explain anything.
